served.stem: Ten runners finish a race and the first three places are recorded in order. How many different orderings of the top three are possible?

answer.line: Ten runners can take first, nine are left for second, eight for third: 10 x 9 x 8 = 720.

steps: Ask the gate question first: does order matter? First, second and third are different places, so swapping two runners makes a new result.
Fill the slots one at a time. 10 runners can take first. One is gone, so 9 can take second, then 8 can take third.
Multiply the choices: 10 x 9 x 8 = 720. Slots multiply. They never add.

choices.note: 10 + 3 adds the runners to the places. Each slot multiplies the choices, so the count grows fast.
30 counts the ways to put one runner in one place: 10 x 3. A finish fills all three places from a shrinking pool: 10, then 9, then 8.
120 counts the groups of three with order ignored. Each group lines up 3 x 2 x 1 = 6 ways, and 120 x 6 = 720.
10 x 10 x 10 lets one runner take two places. Once a runner places, they leave the pool.

student.lockIt: Order matters: multiply the shrinking pool, slot by slot. Order ignored: divide out the orders.
